bib.title: XML retrieval (Chapter 10, Introduction to Information Retrieval)
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition 2009 draft, April 1, 2009)

question: How can ranked retrieval be adapted to structured (XML) documents, including which unit to index and return, how to score, and how to evaluate?
contributions: Challenges of structured retrieval: returned unit, indexing unit, nested elements, context-specific idf, schema heterogeneity (Sec 10.2)
Vector space model over structural terms with context resemblance, SimNoMerge and SimMerge (Sec 10.3)

limits: Book states there is no consensus on the best structured retrieval method and that XQuery-based ranked retrieval is hard to make fast (p.196, 215, 216).
The vector space model is a teaching sketch, not state of the art (p.206); SimMerge details are deferred to references.

Table 10.3 gives mean/median AP but no run counts, significance tests or comparison to unstructured retrieval; Table 10.4 is taken from Kamps et al. 2006 on a subset of CAS topics, not described further.

The chapter assumes XML trees with text at leaves; it does not cover HTML specifics, embeddings, neural retrieval, or LLM chunking. Dated 2008: INEX moved to exhaustivity/specificity and Wikipedia collection (p.211, 216); focused retrieval measures and passage retrieval are still active (p.217).
Authors concede overlap/redundancy is not handled by the Q-based measure (p.213) and that the most relevant passage often does not coincide with an XML element (p.217).
practices: Index units: pseudodocuments, largest element then drill down, leaves then extend, or all elements; each has a flaw (non-coherent, relevance of parent poor predictor of child and vice versa, redundancy) (p.202-203, Sec 10.2).
Restrict eligible return elements: discard small elements, types users do not view, types assessors do not judge relevant, or types a librarian deems useful (p.203).
Collapse nested hits and highlight query terms; show the medium-sized element rather than both section and paragraph, which also gives context (p.203).
Compute idf per XML-context/term pair, but use only the parent node to avoid sparse statistics (p.204).
Treat all queries as extended (descendant) queries and structural constraints as hints: rank mismatches lower, do not drop them (p.205, 207, 217).
Handle relational attribute constraints by pre- or post-filtering (p.200).
Use grade-based relevance with coverage dimension (exact, too small, too large) for element evaluation (p.212).
Use a relational database when text fields are short, exact matching suffices and unordered results are fine (p.215).

terms.definition: search over structured documents; in this book always refers to XML retrieval
A system should always retrieve the most specific part of a document answering the query.
the document unit used in indexing and retrieval
elements that are contained within each other
query in which all parent-child relationships are interpreted as descendant relationships with any number of intervening nodes
a pair of XML-context c and vocabulary term t, written <c, t>
CR(cq,cd) = (1+|cq|)/(1+|cd|) if cq matches cd else 0
cosine variant summing CR-weighted term weights, keeping XML contexts separate for weighting
relaxed variant: pooled statistics across resembling contexts, merged structural terms, relaxed CR
content-only (keyword) vs content-and-structure topics in INEX
exact, too small, too large or no coverage of the retrieved element
several XML schemas occur in one collection, so comparable elements differ in name or structure
text-centric: text dominates, ranked inexact matching; data-centric: numeric attribute-value data, exact matching, stored in databases
retrieval that avoids returning nested elements sharing common subelements
system returns short passages instead of documents

code.snippet: CR(cq, cd) = (1+|cq|)/(1+|cd|) if cq matches cd, 0 otherwise

SCOREDOCUMENTSWITHSIMNOMERGE(q, B, V, N, normalizer): for each <cq,t> in q: wq <- WEIGHT(q,t,cq); for each c in B with CR(cq,c)>0: for each posting of <c,t>: score[docID] += CR(cq,c)*wq*weight(posting); then score[n] /= normalizer[n]
